column2: Tell me of the man, Muse, the man of many turns, who very much
was driven off course, after he had sacked the holy citadel of Troy;
and of many men he saw the cities and came to know their mind,
and many pains he suffered on the sea in his own heart,
striving to win his own life and the homecoming of his comrades.
But not even so did he save his comrades, though he longed to;
for by their own recklessness they perished,
fools, who the cattle of Hyperion Helios
devoured; and he took from them the day of their homecoming.
Of these things, from some point at least, goddess, daughter of Zeus, tell us too.
Then all the others, as many as had escaped sheer destruction,
were at home, having escaped both war and the sea;
but him alone, longing for his homecoming and for his wife,
the nymph, the lady Calypso, bright among goddesses, held back
in her hollow caves, desiring him to be her husband.
But when the year came, as the seasons rolled round,
in which the gods had spun for him to return home
to Ithaca, not even there was he free of trials,
even among his own dear ones. And the gods pitied him, all of them,
except Poseidon; but he raged unceasingly
against godlike Odysseus, until he reached his own land.
But he had gone among the Ethiopians, who are far away,
the Ethiopians who are divided in two, the farthest of men,
some where Hyperion sets, and some where he rises,
to receive a hecatomb of bulls and of rams.
There he was taking delight in the feast, sitting by; but the others
were gathered together in the halls of Olympian Zeus.
And among them the father of men and gods began to speak;
for he remembered in his heart blameless Aegisthus, // ἀμύμονος "blameless": a stock epithet, not moral praise
whom Agamemnon's son, far-famed Orestes, had slain;
remembering him, he spoke words among the immortals:

Oh for shame, how mortals now blame the gods!

34	by their own recklessness have pains beyond their portion,
35	as now Aegisthus, beyond his portion, of Atreides
36	married the wedded wife, and killed him on his return,
37	knowing of sheer destruction, since we told him beforehand,
38	sending Hermes, the keen-sighted Argeiphontes,
39	neither to kill the man himself nor to woo his wife;
40	for from Orestes vengeance shall come for Atreides,
41	when he comes of age and longs for his own land.
42	So spoke Hermes, but the mind of Aegisthus
43	he did not persuade, though he meant him well; and now he has paid for it all at once.
And then the goddess answered him, grey-eyed Athena:

O our father, son of Kronos, highest of rulers,
46	surely that man lies in a destruction he deserved;
47	so may any other perish too, whoever does such things!
48	But my heart is torn for wise-hearted Odysseus,
49	ill-fated, who long now, far from his friends, suffers miseries
50	on a sea-girt island, where is the navel of the sea.
51	An island with trees, and on it a goddess has her dwelling,
52	daughter of Atlas the baleful-minded, who of the sea,
53	all of it, knows the depths, and himself holds the pillars,
54	the tall ones, which keep earth and heaven apart.
55	His daughter holds back the wretched, grieving man,
56	and ever with soft and wheedling words
57	she charms him, so that he may forget Ithaca; but Odysseus,
58	longing to see even the smoke leaping up
59	from his own land, desires to die. And yet not even in you
60	is your own heart moved, Olympian. Did not Odysseus
61	beside the ships of the Argives please you, offering sacrifices
62	in wide Troy? Why then are you so angry with him, Zeus? // ὠδύσαο "you were angry" plays on the name Odysseus
And answering her spoke cloud-gathering Zeus:

My child, what a word has escaped the fence of your teeth!
65	How then could I forget godlike Odysseus,
66	who is beyond mortals in mind, and beyond them has given sacrifices to the gods,
67	the immortals, who hold the wide heaven?
68	But Poseidon the earth-holder is ever unrelentingly
69	angry because of the Cyclops, whom he blinded of his eye,
70	godlike Polyphemus, whose strength is greatest
71	among all the Cyclopes; and the nymph Thoosa bore him,
72	daughter of Phorcys, ruler of the unharvested sea, // ἀτρυγέτοιο: unharvested/barren" or "unresting"; disputed
having lain with Poseidon in hollow caves.
Since then Odysseus, Poseidon the earth-shaker
does not kill at all, but drives him wandering from his native land.
But come, let us here, all of us, take thought
of his homecoming, how he may come; and Poseidon will let go
his anger; for he will not be able at all, against all
the immortal gods, against their will, to quarrel alone."
And then the goddess answered him, grey-eyed Athena:

O our father, son of Kronos, highest of rulers,
82	if indeed this is now dear to the blessed gods,
83	that wise Odysseus should return to his own house,
84	then Hermes, the guide, Argeiphontes,
85	to the island Ogygia let us send, so that with all speed
86	he may tell the fair-tressed nymph our unerring resolve,
87	the homecoming of steadfast-hearted Odysseus, that he may return;
88	and I will go to Ithaca, so that his son
89	I may rouse the more and put strength in his heart,
90	to call to assembly the long-haired Achaeans
91	and speak out to all the suitors, who ever
92	slaughter his thronging sheep and his shambling, crook-horned cattle.
93	And I will send him to Sparta and to sandy Pylos
94	to learn of his dear father's homecoming, if perhaps he may hear of it,
95	and so that good fame among men may be his.
So saying she bound beneath her feet her beautiful sandals,
immortal, golden, which carried her both over the wet sea
and over the boundless land, together with the breaths of the wind;
and she took her mighty spear, pointed with sharp bronze,
heavy, great, stout, with which she subdues the ranks of men,
of heroes, with whom she is angry, she of the mighty father.
And she went down from the peaks of Olympus, darting,
and stood in the land of Ithaca at the front gate of Odysseus,
on the threshold of the courtyard; and in her palm she held the bronze spear,
in the likeness of a stranger, the leader of the Taphians, Mentes.
And she found the proud suitors. They then
with draughts-pieces in front of the doors were delighting their hearts,
sitting on the hides of oxen which they themselves had killed;
and heralds and busy attendants, for them,
some were mixing wine and water in mixing-bowls,
and others again with many-holed sponges the tables
were washing and setting out, and others were portioning out much meat.
Her by far the first to see was godlike Telemachus,
for he was sitting among the suitors, grieved in his own heart,
seeing in his mind his noble father, if from somewhere coming
he might make a scattering of the suitors through the house,
and himself have honour and rule over his own house.
Thinking these things, sitting among the suitors, he saw Athena.
And he went straight to the porch, and was indignant in his heart
that a stranger should stand long at the doors; and standing near
he took her right hand and received the bronze spear,
and speaking to her he addressed winged words:

Welcome, stranger, with us you will be made welcome; and then,
124	when you have tasted dinner, you will tell what you need.
So saying he led the way, and she followed, Pallas Athena.
And when they were inside the lofty house,
the spear he carried and stood against a tall pillar,
inside a well-polished spear-stand, where other
spears of steadfast-hearted Odysseus stood, many,
and her he led and seated on a chair, spreading a linen cloth beneath,
a beautiful, richly wrought one; and beneath was a footstool for the feet.
And beside it he set himself an inlaid seat, apart from the other
suitors, lest the stranger, vexed by the din,
should lose his taste for the dinner, having come among overbearing men,
and so that he might ask him about his father who was gone.
And a handmaid poured water for the hands from a pitcher, bringing it,
a beautiful golden one, over a silver basin,
to wash; and beside them she drew up a polished table.
And the respected housekeeper brought bread and set it before them,
adding many dishes, giving freely from what was at hand;
and a carver lifted and set before them platters of meats
of every kind, and beside them set golden cups;
and a herald went often to and fro among them pouring wine.
And in came the proud suitors. They then
sat down in rows on the couches and chairs,
and for them heralds poured water over their hands,
and maidservants heaped bread beside them in baskets,
and young men filled the mixing-bowls brim-full of drink.
And they put forth their hands to the good things lying ready before them.
But when they had put from them the desire for drink and food,
the suitors, in their minds other things were a care,
song and dance; for these are the adornments of a feast.
And a herald put into the hands the very beautiful lyre
of Phemius, who sang among the suitors by compulsion.
He, playing the lyre, struck up the prelude to sing beautifully.
But Telemachus spoke to grey-eyed Athena,
holding his head near, so that the others might not hear:

Dear stranger, will you be angry with me for what I say?

Therefore I will tell you, stranger, very truly.

marvelled in his heart; for he thought it was a god.
And at once he went among the suitors, a godlike man.
And for them the famous singer was singing, and they in silence
sat listening; and he sang of the homecoming of the Achaeans,
the woeful one, which from Troy Pallas Athena laid upon them.

And they, to dance and to delightful song
turning, took their delight, and waited for evening to come.
And as they took delight, black evening came on;
then, to lie down, they went home, each one.
And Telemachus, where his chamber, in the very beautiful courtyard,
had been built high, in a place seen from all round,
there went to his bed, pondering many things in his mind.
And with him, blazing torches, she carried, she of trusty mind,
Eurycleia, daughter of Ops, son of Peisenor,
whom once Laertes bought with his own possessions
when she was still in her first youth, and he gave the worth of twenty oxen,
and he honoured her equally with his trusty wife in the halls,
but never lay with her in bed, and shunned his wife's anger;
she carried the blazing torches with him, and she most
of the maidservants loved him, and had nursed him when he was little.
He opened the doors of the close-built chamber,
sat on the bed, and took off his soft tunic,
and put it into the hands of the shrewd old woman.
She, folding and smoothing the tunic,
hanging it on a peg beside the corded bed,
went out of the chamber, and pulled the door to by the handle,
the silver one, and drew the bolt home by its strap.
There he, all night long, covered with the finest of sheep's wool,
pondered in his mind the journey that Athena had shown him.
